distractor_pulls.are revised: "atlas" ends in -s and an atlas is a collection of many maps, and the plural "dust trails" sits right before the blank.
distractor_pulls.was revised: The first finite verb a reader meets inside the conditional is the past "logged"; a student who copies the conditional's tense from it writes the past, and the real verb "turns" is eleven words from the blank.
distractor_pulls.were revised: It fits the -s look of "atlas" and the adjacent "trails", follows the past "logged", and "were" beside an "if" looks like the subjunctive students are taught to use in conditionals.

distractor_kills.are revised: Subject-verb agreement: "atlas" is singular (plural "atlases"); correct in "the atlases of one comet's dust trails are revised...".
distractor_kills.was revised: Tense sequence: a past result cannot pair with the present condition "turns out"; correct with "if a fragment that the survey cameras logged turned out to stray".
distractor_kills.were revised: Both rules; correct in "the atlases ... were revised ... if a fragment ... turned out to stray".

distractor_pulls.was losing: The singular "hospital" is the word right before the blank, and "the water main to the hospital" reads as one supply line.
distractor_pulls.have been losing: The passage closes on an ongoing present repair ("is replacing"), so a continuing loss reads naturally as present perfect progressive; it has the right number, and the definite-past phrase is ten words away and is built on a possessive ("last winter's") that reads like a description rather than a date.
distractor_pulls.has been losing: It takes both pulls at once: the adjacent singular "hospital" and the ongoing-problem reading set up by "is replacing".

distractor_kills.was losing: Subject-verb agreement: "mains" is plural; correct in "the water main from the reservoir to the hilltop hospital was losing...".
distractor_kills.have been losing: A present perfect cannot take the definite past adverbial "at the height of last winter's cold snap"; correct in "the mains have been losing pressure" with no past anchor.
distractor_kills.has been losing: Both rules; correct in "the main ... has been losing pressure" with no past anchor.

frame: fronted singular locative, singular head + subject relative clause (no own subject) whose object is plural, blank, phrase, while-clause whose subject is followed by a participial phrase before the present verb

distractor_pulls.are being calibrated: The plural "aftershocks" sits directly before the blank and is the noun the whole passage is about.
distractor_pulls.was being calibrated: Every verb form before the decider is past ("struck", "captured", "recorded") and the first word after the while-clause's subject is the past form "puzzled"; a reader who reads "while station scientists, puzzled" as the time clause's verb copies the past.
distractor_pulls.were being calibrated: It joins the adjacent plural "aftershocks" to the past run of "recorded" and "puzzled".

distractor_kills.are being calibrated: Subject-verb agreement: "seismometer" is singular; correct in "the seismometers that recorded ... are being calibrated".
distractor_kills.was being calibrated: Tense: a past progressive cannot be simultaneous with the present while-clause verb "sort"; correct with "while station scientists ... sorted out".
distractor_kills.were being calibrated: Both rules; correct in "the seismometers ... were being calibrated ... while station scientists sorted out".

distractor_pulls.is sampling its: The sentence opens on a singular subject with a singular "has begun", and the fronted locative pushes the true plural subject out of the usual position, so a student who has fixed "its" on the vent keeps the verb singular too.
distractor_pulls.are sampling their: The plural verb invites a plural pronoun, and "the older craters" are a natural source of emissions, named in the same clause just before the subject.
distractor_pulls.is sampling their: It pairs the singular pull of the vent on the verb with the craters as the emissions' source, each half resolved against a different nearby noun.

distractor_kills.are sampling their: Pronoun-antecedent agreement: the emissions come from the singular "lone active vent"; correct in "The island's active vents have begun erupting, and ... survey teams ... are sampling their emissions".
distractor_kills.is sampling their: Both rules; correct in "Two vents have begun erupting, and ... a survey team ... is sampling their emissions".

frame: opening although-clause in sentence 2: singular subject + appositive, blank; main clause: plural subject + participial phrase whose -ed form reads as a past finite verb, then the present lexical verb
decider_quote: discharge water at a nearly constant rate
deletion_test: Delete "discharge water at a nearly constant rate": nothing says what the geyser lacks, and "scattered" would be read as the main verb, so be, present do and past forms all become possible; the auxiliary is undecidable. No other sentence supplies the elided verb.

distractor_pulls.do not: The plural "springs" is the first noun after the blank and the borrowed verb "discharge" has the plural form, so a student copying the main clause's auxiliary exactly writes "do not".
distractor_pulls.was not: "scattered" is the first verb-like word in the main clause and reads as a past finite verb, the whole passage around the sentence is past narrative ("gauged", "came"), and an "Although X ___," clause most often ends in a be-predicate.
distractor_pulls.were not: It matches the plural "springs" and the past look of "scattered" and of the surrounding narrative.

distractor_kills.do not: Auxiliary agreement: the although-clause's subject "geyser" is singular; correct in "Although the basin's tallest geysers ... do not, the hot springs ... discharge...".
distractor_kills.was not: Ellipsis: the omitted predicate is the lexical "discharge water," which takes do-support, and "discharge" is present; correct in "Although the geyser was not steady, the springs were".
distractor_kills.were not: Do-support needed and "geyser" is singular; correct in "Although the geysers were not, the springs were steady".

distractor_pulls.is dangerous: The first verb inside the each-time clause is the present "track", and sentence 1 states a present rule about glare near airports, so a present hazard statement reads naturally; the past "struck" is seventeen words on.

distractor_pulls.were covering them: The compound subject is plural and a plural verb invites a plural pronoun, and "the neighboring wind farms" sits right before the blank as a plural thing that crews in winter might cover.

frame: clause 1 ends on a singular noun (scar); clause 2 opens with a noun phrase + participial phrase readable as its appositive or colon elaboration (a crescent of bare rock rising above the debris field); clause 2's verb arrives 10 words after the blank
structure: Left: an independent clause ending "left a jagged scar". Right: an independent clause whose subject "a crescent of bare rock rising above the debris field" is followed by the finite verb "drew" (unambiguously past, not a participle); the second clause is a later event, not an elaboration.
decider_quote: drew climbers and geologists from across the state within a decade

distractor_pulls.scar, a: Up to "field" the noun phrase is a natural appositive describing the scar ("a jagged scar, a crescent of bare rock rising above the debris field"), and the participle "rising" keeps the description going.
distractor_pulls.scar: a: A colon before a phrase that describes what the scar looks like is standard ("left a jagged scar: a crescent of bare rock..."), and the participle makes the elaboration reading even more natural.
distractor_pulls.scar a: A reader who senses the boundary but treats "scar" as running straight into a modifier, as in "a scar a kilometer wide", leaves the gap unmarked.

distractor_kills.scar, a: Comma splice: "drew" makes the right side an independent clause, and a comma cannot join two independent clauses.
distractor_kills.scar: a: A colon introduces an explanation, list or elaboration of what precedes; "a crescent ... drew climbers ... within a decade" reports a later event.
distractor_kills.scar a: Fused sentence: two independent clauses with no punctuation or conjunction.
